items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: The interviewee mentions Benny Goodman only in the context of the interviewer's story about a 1936 broadcast ('...and Benny Goodman as the end.'), with no personal interaction or relationship described by the interviewee.

ctx.x: Fletcher Henderson and Benny Morton of Kansas City were also among the first swing artists. Benny Morton's name is spelled M-O-R-T-O-N. Do you want me to read the letter to the editor? Just a moment.

These Negroes showed their appreciation after I had made it easy for them to come up and open his publishing concern. He didn't know me. That 20 years had passed. In 1936, Lou Gensler had a big broadcast. He tried to locate us to put us in the beginning and Benny Goodman as the end. In other words, the beginning and end. At this time, all these prophets got up in arms against us. John Hammond was one of them. He worked for Handy, I suppose, some kind of cheap lawyer or something on that order. And Handy was given…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: Benny Goodman was in the center then. And what he played, if you look at it, the St. Louis Blues is a copy for my cornet part and also Larry Shields' clarinet part. He had mixed to listen to the records of the original Lixieland Jazz Band when he was only eight years old.

ctx.x: Yeah, but how long, I mean when was the last time though?

In 1938 I reorganized the band. When this music was being taken away from New Orleans, they were calling Chicago Swing. Benny Goodman was in the center then. And what he played, if you look at it, the St. Louis Blues is a copy for my cornet part and also Larry Shields' clarinet part. He had mixed to listen to the records of the original Lixieland Jazz Band when he was only eight years old. And I played, when I first started playing in a group, it would have been about 1904.
